summary: Teach 11-13s how astronomers detect planets around other stars indirectly, by reading effects on the STAR rather than seeing the planet. The core conceptual move is inferring an unseen cause from a measured signal. Centre the work on two methods: (1) the TRANSIT method — a planet crossing in front of its star makes starlight dip by a tiny, repeating amount, where dip DEPTH encodes planet size (relative to the star) and dip SPACING encodes orbital period; (2) RADIAL VELOCITY — a planet's gravity tugs the star into a small wobble about the system's centre of mass, shifting its light bluer (approaching) then redder (receding). Layer on the habitable zone (orbital band where liquid water could exist) and biosignatures (atmospheric gas combinations out of equilibrium, e.g. oxygen with methane, that might hint at life). Stress necessary-not-sufficient reasoning: habitable zone is candidacy not confirmation, and one gas is not proof of life.
misconceptions: 'We take photos of the planets' — almost all exoplanets are found indirectly; direct images are rare and show dots, not worlds
'A dip in brightness means the star is dimming/dying' — it is a temporary, repeating eclipse by an orbiting planet, not a change in the star
'In the habitable zone = has life / has water' — the zone only means liquid water is possible given the right atmosphere; it is a candidacy, not a confirmation
'Radial velocity means the star is really moving toward us across space' — it is a tiny back-and-forth wobble about the system's centre of mass, read from spectral shifts
'Bigger dip = closer planet' — dip DEPTH tracks planet SIZE relative to the star; orbital distance shows up in the PERIOD (spacing of dips), not the depth
'One gas proves life' — biosignatures rely on combinations out of chemical equilibrium (e.g. oxygen plus methane together), and even then are debated

activities.title: Build the planet, watch its light-curve fingerprint
steps: Drag a small planet onto an orbit around a star; below, a brightness-vs-time line traces across the screen in real time as the planet crosses in front of the star — flat line (star alone), a dip (planet crossing), flat again
Grab a SIZE control and watch the dip get DEEPER as the planet grows; grab an ORBIT RADIUS / PERIOD control and watch the SPACING between dips stretch out and transits grow rarer
State in your own words which graph feature encodes planet size and which encodes orbital period
Enter 'detective mode', which hides the planet and gives you only a wiggly light curve: set size and period to reconstruct the planet that must have produced it

Flip a RADIAL-VELOCITY toggle to see the same planet betrayed a second way — the star wobbling about the system's centre of mass, its spectrum shifting blue (approaching) then red (receding), plotted on a second graph
activities.insight: We never see the planet; we read its fingerprints on the star's light. Dip DEPTH tracks planet SIZE relative to the star, while orbital distance shows up in the PERIOD (spacing of dips), not the depth. Two independent signals (transit and wobble) can reveal the same unseen world.

activities.title: Name the parts of a light curve and the Goldilocks band
steps: Study a labelled light curve (flat–dip–flat) and identify the moment of crossing, the depth of the dip, and the gap between dips
Reveal that the dip corresponds to the planet crossing (a deeper dip means a bigger planet compared with its star) and the gap between dips corresponds to the orbit time (period)
Examine a habitable-zone band diagram — a star with a coloured 'Goldilocks' ring at the right distance — and state the definition: 'not too hot, not too cold for liquid water'
Inspect a transmission-spectrum 'barcode' showing dark lines where an atmosphere's gases absorb light, and read off which gases a spectrum reveals
activities.insight: Lock the vocabulary: dip depth, dip spacing/period, habitable zone, transmission spectrum. Naming the parts supports, but does not replace, reasoning about why depth and spacing encode different things.

activities.title: Read-the-graph consolidation challenges
steps: Match a given light curve to the planet that produced it, choosing from several candidates
Identify which graph feature encodes size and which encodes period
Set the dip depth for a Jupiter-sized versus an Earth-sized planet orbiting the same Sun-like star

Match each tool to what it measures: transit → size, radial velocity → mass (on its own only a lower limit, but a true mass when the planet also transits); and explain that together they give density and hence rough composition (rocky vs gas)
Answer a question on the oxygen+methane biosignature logic: why two out-of-equilibrium gases together are a stronger hint than either alone
activities.insight: Transit gives size, radial velocity gives mass, and the two together give density and hence a rough idea of composition (rocky vs gas). Consolidating the read-the-graph skill confirms the learner can apply the depth/period distinction rather than merely recognise it.

activities.title: In role: hunting a real candidate signal
steps: Take on the role of an exoplanet hunter talking with a mission scientist who walks you through a real candidate signal (e.g. a Kepler/TESS light curve, or the 51 Pegasi b wobble)
Explain what you would measure next to confirm the signal really is a planet, and why the pattern needs to REPEAT periodically
Discuss why dips are often less than 1% of the star's brightness, and why measuring something so faint so precisely is the real achievement (and why space telescopes help)
activities.insight: Confirmation needs a repeating, periodic signal, because a single one-off dim is not enough. Even a repeating signal must be checked against other causes, often with a second method such as radial velocity. Framing detection as forensic reasoning builds the habit of inferring an unseen cause from a measured signal using real discovery data.

checkQuestion: Astronomers announce they've found a planet orbiting a star hundreds of light-years away — but they never actually took a picture of the planet itself. How can they know it's there? And if they later detect oxygen in its air, does that prove there's life? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: They detect the planet INDIRECTLY, from its effect on the star, not by photographing it. In the transit method, the planet crossing in front of its star causes a tiny, regular DIP in the star's brightness each orbit; in the radial-velocity method, the planet's gravity makes the star WOBBLE slightly, shifting its light toward red then blue (Doppler). The repeating, periodic pattern is what confirms it's a planet. As for oxygen: on its own it doesn't prove life, because some non-living processes make it too. Far more telling is finding gases TOGETHER that shouldn't coexist unless something keeps replenishing them — oxygen AND methane at once — which would strongly hint at active life. And a planet must be in the habitable zone (where liquid water could exist) to be a promising place to look.
